status_definitions.exact: Matches the verified identity, meaning and printed order.
status_definitions.close: Same verified meaning, but wording has been paraphrased or the title is broader/narrower.
status_definitions.unsupported: No evidence that this material is the official text; replacement is explicitly original mock material.
status_definitions.conflict: Wrong version/topic, missing or substituted item, or material change in printed order.

methodology.copyright_rule: Official context passages are not reproduced. Every replacement context is newly written, 150–220 words, and explicitly labelled as mock/adapted practice material.
methodology.stable_id_rule: Existing set_id, point_id and question_id values are preserved. Because canonical 1.1 and 1.3 are swapped, their stable set_id slugs remain semantically misleading; migration should not silently rename them.

key_findings: The canonical 2023 version 1.1 and 1.3 topics are reversed. Printed 1.1 is Unmanned Convenience Stores; printed 1.3 is Plant-Based Meats.
The 24 past-paper versions are real and complete for 1.1–8.3. No missing or extra past-paper version was found.
Many Part A prompts preserve the topic but use candidate-recall paraphrases rather than printed wording.
Part B order/content conflicts are material in 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 3.1, 4.2, 4.3, 5.1, 5.2 and 5.3.
Current generic contexts are not supported as official passages. All 24 replacements are original, topic-specific mock contexts.
The one hidden wearable mock is internally coherent and correctly hidden, but its current context is shorter than the 150–220-word audit standard.

replacement.title: Unmanned Convenience Stores
replacement.source_note: Past-paper practice based on the cross-referenced 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 1.1 topic and printed prompt order. The context is original mock material, not the official HKEAA passage. Task and question wording is lightly adapted for practice.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 1.1 topic:
context.title: A Store with No Cashier
body: A convenience-store chain is testing a small branch inside a busy railway station. Cameras and shelf sensors record what customers pick up, while a payment screen prepares the bill automatically. Shoppers can pay by card, phone or cash before an exit gate opens. One employee remains on site to restock shelves, answer questions and help customers when the system fails.

Supporters say the shop can operate for longer hours and reduce queues, especially when commuters are in a hurry. The company can also use sales data to keep popular products in stock. However, the branch offers fewer products than a normal store, and some customers worry about privacy, inaccurate bills and what happens if they need help. Others fear that automated stores will reduce entry-level jobs.

Retail analysts add that Hong Kong presents special challenges: shops are crowded, customers include tourists and elderly people, and electronic systems must cope with several payment methods. A successful unmanned shop may therefore need clear instructions, reliable security and staff who can respond quickly from nearby.

part_a.instruction: Your group is doing a project on unmanned convenience stores. Discuss the following points.

discussion_points.text: the benefits of unmanned convenience stores
the limitations of unmanned convenience stores
whether unmanned convenience stores are a good idea for Hong Kong
anything else you think is important

part_b.instruction: The examiner will ask you one or more questions based on Part A. You will have up to 1 minute to respond.

questions.text: Do you often shop at convenience stores?
What do people usually buy at a convenience store?
Do you prefer self-checkout or paying a cashier?
Is customer service important to you when shopping?
Do you think there will be more theft in unmanned stores?
Would you find shopping at an unmanned store too impersonal?
Do you think the trend of unmanned stores will continue to grow?
Do you think automation is making life too convenient?

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 1.2 topic:
context.title: Is This the End of Cinemas?
body: Movie streaming has changed how audiences choose entertainment. For one monthly fee, viewers can watch a large library of films at home or on a mobile device. They can pause a film, choose subtitles and avoid travel. New releases also reach online platforms more quickly than before, so some people visit cinemas less often.

Cinemas still offer an experience that a living room cannot easily copy. A large screen, powerful sound and a shared audience can make a film feel like a special event. Friends may also combine a cinema visit with a meal or shopping. Yet tickets and snacks are expensive, popular screenings sell out, and travelling home after a late film can be inconvenient.

Local cinema operators are experimenting with loyalty programmes, student prices, comfortable seats and special screenings. Some show classic films, sports events or question-and-answer sessions with filmmakers. Their challenge is to give audiences a reason to leave home while keeping prices affordable and ensuring that smaller, less commercial films can still reach the public.

anything else you think is important

Do you think movie streaming services will eventually replace cinemas?

context.title: Plant-Based Food Meets Cantonese Cooking
body: Plant-based meat is now appearing in dishes that once depended on pork, beef or seafood. A Hong Kong restaurant has tested meat-free versions of familiar Cantonese dishes, using products made from beans, grains and vegetable oils. Its chefs say that flavour and texture are important because diners may reject a sustainable choice if it does not feel satisfying.

Interest in these products is driven by several concerns. Some consumers want more vegetarian choices, while others hope to reduce the environmental impact of livestock farming. Health is another reason, although nutritionists warn that plant-based products can still contain high levels of salt or fat. They should be compared carefully rather than assumed to be healthy.

A secondary school is considering serving plant-based meals in its canteen on Green Mondays. Supporters believe students could discover new food and think about climate change. Critics worry about price, food waste and whether the dishes respect students’ cultural preferences. The school must decide whether to encourage participation, require it or offer plant-based food beside the usual menu.

replacement.source_note: Past-paper practice based on the cross-referenced 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 2.1 topic and printed prompt order. The context is original mock material, not the official HKEAA passage. Task and question wording is lightly adapted for practice.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 2.1 topic:
context.title: Different Body Clocks at Work
body: Some people feel most alert early in the morning, while others naturally become energetic late at night. These patterns are partly influenced by habits and partly by the body’s internal clock. Problems arise when a person’s preferred schedule does not match school or work. A night owl who must start at eight o’clock may lose sleep even when trying to go to bed earlier.

Regular sleep matters. Too little sleep can affect concentration, mood and long-term health. Early risers may find it easier to follow normal timetables and exercise before the day becomes busy. Night owls, however, may enjoy quiet hours for creative work and can be highly productive when interruptions are limited.

Some employers are testing flexible starting times or allowing staff to work from home. Supporters say performance should matter more than the hour at which someone arrives. Managers worry that different schedules may make teamwork and customer service harder. Any flexible system would need shared meeting hours, clear deadlines and rules to prevent employees from working late and starting early at the same time.

part_a.instruction: Your group is doing a project on sleeping patterns. Discuss the following points.

discussion_points.text: the advantages of being a night owl
the advantages of getting up early
whether companies should offer flexible working hours for people with different sleeping patterns
anything else you think is important

part_b.instruction: The examiner will ask you one or more questions based on Part A. You will have up to 1 minute to respond.

questions.text: Do you wake up early on weekends?
Do you often have problems waking up in the morning?
What do you do if you cannot fall asleep?

Have you ever overslept and missed something important?
What time of day are you most productive?
Would you consider a job that requires working at night?
Do you envy people who need only a few hours of sleep?

replacement.title: Teachers and Students on Social Media
replacement.source_note: Past-paper practice based on the cross-referenced 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 2.2 topic and printed prompt order. The context is original mock material, not the official HKEAA passage. Task and question wording is lightly adapted for practice.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 2.2 topic:
context.title: Should Teachers and Students Be Online Friends?
body: Social media can make communication between teachers and students quick and familiar. A teacher may post reminders, share useful links or answer simple questions after school. Some students also feel more comfortable asking for help online than speaking in front of a class. Used carefully, a class account can strengthen learning and allow positive role models to reach students where they already spend time.

Personal accounts create different problems. Informal messages can blur the boundary between friendship and professional communication. Students may see private photographs or opinions that were never intended for a school audience, while teachers may learn more about students’ social lives than is appropriate. Screenshots can spread beyond the intended group, and a late-night message may create unrealistic expectations about when teachers must reply.

A school is considering a policy that would stop teachers and students from connecting through personal accounts. Official class accounts would remain available and all messages would be visible to the school. The proposal may protect both sides, but it could also remove a useful channel unless the school offers a practical alternative.

part_a.instruction: Your school is considering a policy that would not allow teachers and students to be friends on social media. Discuss the proposal.

discussion_points.text: why students like to connect with teachers on social media

anything else you think is important

Do you think many Hong Kong teachers are active on social media?
Why do you think Instagram is so popular?
Should schools teach students how to use social media safely?
Should parents monitor their children’s friends on social media?
Does social media negatively affect your learning?
Should schools monitor their students’ social media activities?

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 2.3 topic:
context.title: Three Unusual Graduation Ideas
body: A local events company has suggested three experiences for a class graduation celebration. The first is a short helicopter flight over Victoria Harbour and the Geopark. It offers excellent photographs but is expensive and can take only a few students at a time. Bad weather may also cause a last-minute cancellation.

The second option is a cooking lesson with a well-known chef. Students would prepare a meal together and then hold a dinner party. The activity is social and can include teachers, although the restaurant has limited space and must know about allergies in advance. The third option is an outdoor zip-line experience. Trained guides provide safety equipment, but participants must travel to the site and some may be afraid of heights.

The class has a fixed budget and wants the celebration to be memorable without excluding anyone. Organisers must consider cost, safety, transport, group size and the meaning of graduation. They may choose one of the suggested activities or design a simpler event at school that allows every student to participate.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 3.1 topic:
context.title: How Staying Home Changed Fashion
body: Periods of working and studying from home changed what many people expected from clothes. Instead of formal outfits, shoppers looked for soft fabrics, loose shapes and items that could be worn for both a video meeting and an evening at home. Some consumers bought fewer clothes because they had fewer social events, while others spent more time browsing online shops.

Social media became an important source of fashion ideas. Short videos showed viewers how to combine comfortable clothes or turn old items into new outfits. At the same time, fast-moving online trends encouraged impulse buying. Customers could order several sizes, return unwanted items and expect rapid delivery, creating extra packaging and transport.

Fashion companies now face mixed expectations. Customers want comfort and low prices, but many also ask for durable products, fair working conditions and less waste. Shops can respond with clearer size information, repair services, recycled materials and collections suitable for flexible work. The challenge is to remain profitable without encouraging people to buy clothes they will rarely wear.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 3.2 topic:
context.title: What Students Learn from Cleaning
body: At some Japanese schools, students spend about twenty minutes cleaning classrooms and shared areas after lunch. Each class receives specific duties, and students work in small groups. The practice is not intended to replace professional cleaners. Instead, it teaches students to care for spaces that everyone uses and to notice the work required to keep a school comfortable.

Teachers say cleaning can develop responsibility, cooperation and respect. A student who must sweep a corridor may be less likely to drop litter there later. Similar benefits can come from household chores: young people feel that they make a useful contribution and learn practical skills. However, poorly organised sessions may become unfair if responsible students do most of the work or if younger pupils are given unsafe tasks.

A Hong Kong school is considering adding short cleaning sessions to its timetable as part of an environmental campaign. It must decide how often sessions should occur, which duties suit different forms and how to provide equipment and supervision. The plan should improve habits without reducing lesson time or allowing cleaning to be used as punishment.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 3.3 topic:
context.title: Gardening as a Way to Feel Better
body: Horticultural therapy uses plants and gardening activities to support physical and mental health. Participants may water seedlings, arrange flowers or grow vegetables. These simple tasks provide a clear routine and a visible result. Time spent in green spaces can also reduce stress, encourage gentle movement and give people a break from screens and crowded indoor environments.

Schools can use gardening in several ways. A small herb garden can support science lessons, while flowers can improve an unattractive corner of the campus. Students may learn patience because plants need regular care, not attention only when an event is approaching. Produce can be used in cooking activities or sold for charity. However, gardens require space, tools, water and a plan for weekends and holidays.

One school wants to develop students’ interest in growing plants as part of a well-being programme. Some students may prefer sports, music or art, so participation should offer different roles such as design, photography and record keeping. The school must decide whether gardening will attract enough interest and how it can complement other activities rather than replace them.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 4.1 topic:
context.title: More than a Smartwatch
body: Wearable technology now includes rings, bracelets, clothing and shoes as well as smartwatches. A smart ring can collect information about sleep, movement and heart rate without displaying messages. Sensor-equipped clothing covers more of the body and may provide useful information about breathing, posture or exercise technique. Athletes and patients may therefore benefit from data collected throughout the day.

The same devices raise questions. Measurements are not always accurate, and users may worry unnecessarily about a single unusual result. Companies can collect location and health data that people would normally keep private. Wearables are also expensive and may become outdated quickly. In schools, a watch that receives messages can distract students or provide unfair help during a test.

Supporters argue that simple fitness trackers can motivate students to move and help physical-education classes set personal goals. A complete ban may treat every device as if it were a phone. Schools could instead require communication features to be disabled, prohibit devices during tests and explain how health information should be protected.

replacement.title: Adaptability Quotient

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 4.2 topic:
context.title: AQ: Learning to Handle Change
body: People often talk about IQ and emotional intelligence, but employers increasingly discuss adaptability quotient, or AQ. It describes a person’s ability to learn, adjust and keep working when circumstances change. New technology, unexpected events and changing customer needs mean that knowledge learned once may not remain useful for an entire career.

Adaptability does not mean accepting every change without question. It involves noticing what is different, asking for information and testing a sensible response. People can develop it by varying routines, learning unfamiliar skills and listening to viewpoints outside their usual circle. Reflection is also important: after a plan fails, an adaptable person identifies what can be improved instead of simply repeating the same action.

A school is planning an AQ workshop. Some teachers want problem-solving games and surprise challenges, while others prefer talks by people who changed careers or overcame setbacks. Students may feel uncomfortable if activities reward risk-taking without providing support. The workshop therefore needs a safe way to practise change and a clear explanation of how adaptability differs from intelligence, confidence and obedience.

whether adaptability is more important than intelligence
whether adaptability can be taught
anything else you think is important

Do you think change is always good?

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 4.3 topic:
context.title: Using Social Media with Purpose
body: Social media can spread useful knowledge, encourage creativity and help people find communities. It can also fill every quiet moment with comparison, advertising and upsetting news. A feed is selected by both the user and the platform, so it may give a distorted picture of other people’s lives. Popular accounts often show carefully edited highlights rather than ordinary experiences.

Digital-well-being advisers suggest using social media with a purpose. Before opening an app, a user can ask what they need to do and close it afterwards. Unfollowing accounts that create anger or pressure can improve the experience. Turning off unnecessary notifications and keeping phones away during study or sleep also reduces automatic checking. If a platform seriously affects someone’s mood, taking a temporary break may be sensible.

A school Mental Health and Wellness Club wants to promote healthier habits without presenting all social media as harmful. It could run a feed-cleaning workshop, a notification-free challenge or a campaign about realistic posting. The club must make activities supportive rather than judgmental and explain when students should seek help from an adult.

context.title: Finding Family Stories through DNA
body: Home DNA kits have made family-history research easier to begin. A customer sends a small sample to a company and later receives an estimate of where their ancestors may have lived. The result can challenge family assumptions and lead users to old records or distant relatives. For some people, the search provides a stronger sense of identity and preserves stories that might otherwise disappear.

The result is not a complete family history. Estimates depend on the company’s database and may change as more samples are added. Unexpected relatives or information about parentage can cause distress. DNA is also highly personal: once data is stored, users may not fully control whether it is used for research, shared with another company or requested by authorities.

A class project is examining whether DNA tests are a good way to research family history. Alternatives include interviewing relatives, collecting photographs, reading public records and mapping important family events. These methods take time but provide names, choices and experiences that a percentage on a DNA report cannot explain. A careful project should combine evidence and respect relatives who prefer not to participate.

context.title: From Unwanted Items to a School Fund
body: Online marketplaces allow people to photograph an item, write a short description and offer it for sale within minutes. It can also help a small organisation reach more customers than a physical sale.

Online selling also creates risks. A buyer may disappear, claim an item is damaged or send a false payment message. Delivery costs can remove much of the profit from a cheap product. context.title: Why a Story Can Sell a Product
body: Some of the most memorable advertisements do more than list a product’s features. They present a character, a problem and a satisfying ending. Viewers may remember a funny mistake, an unexpected act of kindness or a small personal victory long after they forget the price. If the product helps the story reach its conclusion, the brand becomes connected with that emotion.

Storytelling can also fail. A dramatic story may attract attention while leaving viewers unsure what is being sold. An emotional message can feel dishonest if the product has little connection to it. Celebrities may dominate the advertisement, and a joke that works for one audience may offend another. A good campaign therefore needs a simple idea, a clear audience and a believable role for the product.

A Business Studies class must advertise a new sports drink called Champion. The group could show a student preparing for a difficult race, a team recovering from a mistake or an ordinary person completing a personal challenge. Sound, colour, humour and a short slogan can make the advertisement memorable, but the claims about the drink must remain accurate.

context.source_line: Original mock context written for practice after cross-referencing the 2023 HKDSE Paper 4 version 7.1 topic:
context.title: Is Being Late Always Disrespectful?
body: Ideas about time differ across cultures and situations. In some places, arriving late for a business meeting suggests poor preparation or disrespect. Daily life is organised around calendars, deadlines and exact transport schedules. In other places, relationships and changing circumstances may matter more than a fixed starting time, so an event begins when the necessary people have arrived.

Researchers often describe cultures as fast-paced or slow-paced, but these labels can become stereotypes. A country may value punctual trains while allowing long social meals. Age, occupation and city life also influence behaviour. Mobile phones have changed expectations because people can update one another immediately, yet constant messages may make schedules feel even more demanding.

Hong Kong is often associated with speed, long working hours and the idea that time is money. This can support efficiency, but it may also leave little room for rest, family and unplanned conversation. A slower life does not require ignoring responsibilities. People can protect meal times, reduce unnecessary appointments, walk without checking a phone and agree on which deadlines truly matter.

context.title: When an Online Trend Threatens Wildlife
body: Videos of small wild animals in cafés and private homes can receive millions of views. Their large eyes and unusual behaviour make them appear harmless, and viewers may want the same experience. Wildlife groups warn that online popularity can increase demand, encouraging traders to remove animals from natural habitats and transport them in poor conditions.

A wild animal may survive in a home without living well. It can need a specialised diet, a large territory, contact with its own species and activity at times when an owner wants to sleep. Even a caring person may not recognise illness or stress. Some animals can bite, spread disease or be abandoned when they become difficult to manage. The trade also adds pressure to species already affected by habitat loss.

Social media platforms, cafés and pet sellers all influence what people consider an acceptable pet. Clear labels, restrictions on harmful content and public education may reduce impulsive purchases. Schools can help students distinguish between admiring wildlife and owning it. A responsible choice should consider animal welfare, public safety, conservation and whether a domestic animal can meet the owner’s needs instead.

body: As the world population grows, producing enough protein without using more land and water will become difficult. In many countries, insects have been eaten for generations. Crickets, beetle larvae and other species can contain protein, vitamins and minerals. They also require less space and feed than cattle and can produce far fewer greenhouse-gas emissions.

These advantages do not make insect food an easy choice. People who did not grow up eating insects may feel disgust or worry about safety. Farms need hygiene standards, clear labelling and controls on species and feed. Allergy risks must also be studied. Products may be easier to accept when insects are ground into flour for noodles, snack bars or dumpling fillings rather than served whole.

A group is considering the food people may eat in the future. Promotion could begin with small tastings, chef demonstrations and honest information about nutrition and environmental impact. Price and flavour will matter as much as education. Insect products should be offered as another option, not presented as a punishment or as the only responsible diet.

context.title: Why City Design Changes How Much We Walk
body: A large step-count study found that people in Hong Kong walk more than residents of many other cities. Dense neighbourhoods, frequent public transport and nearby shops mean that walking is often part of an ordinary journey. Research also links regular walking with better heart health, lower stress and a reduced risk of several long-term illnesses. It is free and requires no special equipment.

High average figures can hide important differences. Some districts have steep slopes, narrow pavements or roads that are difficult to cross. Summer heat, heavy rain, poor air quality and crowded streets discourage longer walks. Elderly people, wheelchair users and parents with young children may face broken surfaces or missing lifts that other pedestrians barely notice.

A walking-friendly city needs connected pavements, shade, seating, safe crossings, clear signs and routes that lead somewhere useful. Schools and workplaces can support walking through maps, step challenges and secure places for belongings, but activity should not become unhealthy competition. The group must decide whether Hong Kong’s environment encourages genuine choice or simply makes residents walk out of necessity.

context.source_line: Original mock context for internal practice:
context.title: When Your Watch Knows More About You
body: Smartwatches, rings and sensor-equipped clothing can count steps, measure heart rate and estimate sleep quality. Some devices remind users to move after long periods of sitting, while others send an alert when they detect an unusual pattern. Athletes may use the data to plan training, and patients can show a longer record to a doctor. Continuous information can reveal changes that a short clinic visit might miss.

Wearable data is not always accurate or easy to interpret. A low sleep score may create anxiety even when the user feels well. Personal information may be stored by technology companies, shared with other services or exposed in a data breach. Users may not understand what they accepted when they first set up the device.

Schools face an additional problem because a smartwatch can receive messages and may be used unfairly during tests. A sensible policy could distinguish a basic health tracker from a communication device, restrict wearables during assessments and prohibit schools from collecting fitness data without clear consent. Students should also remember that a gadget offers useful clues, not a medical diagnosis.
